flawed_step: Step 2: From P(X>Y)>1/2 and P(Y>Z)>1/2, one cannot infer P(X>Z)>1/2. Although {X>Y}∩{Y>Z}⊆{X>Z}, the assumptions only guarantee that the intersection has positive probability, not probability greater than 1/2.
counterexample: Roll three mutually independent fair six-sided dice with face values X=(0,0,4,4,4,4), Y=(3,3,3,3,3,3), and Z=(2,2,2,2,6,6). Then P(X>Y)=4/6=2/3>1/2. Also P(Y>Z)=4/6=2/3>1/2. But X>Z occurs exactly when X=4 and Z=2, so P(X>Z)=(4/6)(4/6)=16/36=4/9<1/2. Thus X beats Y and Y beats Z, while X does not beat Z.
assessment_summary: Step 1, unpacking the two hypotheses as probability inequalities, is justified. The attempted transitive inference fails at Step 2, and the explicit independent-dice construction disproves the statement.
